

# A Multilevel Analysis of Government Responses to Internal Displacement

Internal displacement is both an intentional consequence of political violence and an evolving political relationship between citizens and the state, spanning strategic violence, contested legal citizenship, and localised institutional governance (Tarkhanova, 2023; Kalyvas, 2006; Steele, 2017). Increasingly, scholarship has also examined what happens after displacement: states adopt formal policies toward internally displaced people (IDPs), but implementation varies across contexts and policy domains, while informal practices may diverge from formal commitments (Lichtenheld & Steele, 2026). Yet, we know considerably less about the political relationships that explain why governments respond to displaced populations with protection in some circumstances and repression or exclusion in others.

The “Protect and Repress: The Logic of Government Responses to Internal Displacement” (GRID) project conceptualises government responses to internal displacement along this protection-repression continuum and proposes that political alignment among multi-level actors shapes these responses (Steele, Schwartz, & Lichtenheld, 2024). I develop this framework by asking, “How do configurations of political alignment among national governments, local authorities and displaced populations shape the composition of government protection and repression across territories and policy domains?”

This question connects the following strands of literature that have largely developed separately:

I) Research on the politics of displacement demonstrates that state and non-state actors can use population displacement strategically to reshape territorial and political relations (Kalyvas, 2006; Steele, 2017);

II) Scholarship on multilevel governance shows that states are not unitary actors: political incentives and policy implementation can vary across territorial levels, and political alignment between national and subnational governments can affect policy outcomes (Niedzwiecki, 2016);

III) Emerging research on the local governance of internal displacement demonstrates that local authorities can play a decisive role in access to services, political participation and durable solutions, while relationships between IDPs and local governments may develop differently from those established with central states (Weihmayer, 2024). 

Bringing these literatures together makes it possible to examine not simply whether governments are aligned with displaced populations, but how alignment is configured across levels of government and how this configuration translates into specific responses.

I argue that political alignment should not be treated as a uniform or scalar relationship. Its consequences depend on whether alignment is shared across national and local authorities or fragmented between them and on where meaningful authority over a particular policy domain is located. This explains why governments can produce heterogeneous response profiles across territories and domains. I advance three expectations:

H1: Greater alignment among national governments, local authorities, and IDPs will be associated with more protective response profiles. 

H2: Fragmented political alignment is associated with more heterogeneous combinations of protective and repressive responses. 

H3: The relationship between political alignment and government responses varies according to the institutional location of authority over the relevant policy domain. 

Methodologically, I propose an integrated nested design that combines cross-national statistical analysis, subnational quantitative analysis, and qualitative process tracing (Lieberman, 2005; Seawright, 2016; Beach and Pedersen, 2019). First, I will analyse GRID’s cross-national dataset of government responses to internal displacement. The analysis will examine whether variation in political alignment is associated with variation in protective and repressive responses across countries and over time. Depending on the resulting data structure, I will employ panel models with country and temporal fixed effects and, where appropriate, event-study specifications around identifiable changes in political alignment. Analyses will be conducted in R, including i) data harmonisation; ii) model estimation; iii) clustered inference; and iv) reproducible visualisation.

Identification is complicated by the possibility that political alignment affects not only government responses but also the production and composition of displacement itself. I will, therefore, wherever possible, distinguish pre-displacement political alignment from subsequent government responses and distinguish displacement caused by the responding state from displacement it did not cause. Lagged measures, alternative operationalisations and theoretically justified covariates will address temporal ordering and confounding, while robustness and sensitivity analyses will assess dependence on model specification. Because political alignment can take different institutional forms across contexts, measurement validity will be treated as a central methodological concern (Adcock and Collier, 2001).

The cross-national analysis will, potentially, inform a systematic nested strategy. Colombia will provide the principal subnational quantitative analysis, linking the [Registro Único de Víctimas](https://www.unidadvictimas.gov.co/registro-unico-de-victimas-ruv/) with municipal electoral and political data, as well as relevant conflict indicators, in a municipality-year dataset. This will allow analysis of within-country variation while accounting for time-invariant municipal characteristics. Where appropriate, electoral turnover will provide temporal variation for event-study analyses. Importantly, whereas existing research on Colombia has examined how political alignments contributed to the production and targeting of displacement (Steele, 2011; Steele, 2017), I will examine the political determinants of government responses after displacement has occurred.

Iraq and Burundi will provide complementary comparative evidence rather than being treated as statistically equivalent cases. Iraq offers location-level displacement and return data, along with variation in territorial and institutional authority, while Burundi provides a contrasting political context in which comparable quantitative measures of alignment are more limited. I will therefore use available quantitative evidence, alongside qualitative process tracing where feasible, to assess whether mechanisms identified in the statistical analysis carry over across different institutional configurations. This asymmetric design follows the logic of nested analysis rather than treating data availability as a substitute for theoretical case selection (Lieberman, 2005).

Process tracing will examine the mechanisms connecting political alignment to government behaviour, drawing on government and administrative documents, policy records, humanitarian sources and interviews where appropriate (Beach and Pedersen, 2019; Bennett and Checkel, 2015). It will distinguish political explanations from competing accounts based on i) administrative capacity; ii) conflict intensity; and iii) territorial control. The project will thus combine comparative breadth with within-case analysis to clarify when political alignment translates into protection, repression, or both.

The project contributes theoretically by conceptualising political alignment as a multilevel configuration rather than a uniform relationship and examining how these configurations interact with the institutional location of authority to produce different government responses. Empirically, it will extend GRID’s cross-national analysis through subnational evidence and theoretically informed comparative investigation. Most importantly, it will specify how the territorial configuration of political relationships and governmental authority conditions the form that protection and repression take, advancing understanding of both internal displacement and the political determinants of state responses.
